podcast.title: Joined The Police at 36 (1977)
podcast.body: In 1977, after years of working in various musical roles, Andy Summers, then 36, accepted an invitation to join Sting and Stuart Copeland in the newly forming band, The Police, breaking through the following year. "So after bouncing around for years in 1977, he accepted an invitation to join Sting and Stuart Copeland in the police, which was just starting out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Late Bloomers

podcast.title: Lawsuit Against Sting (2025)
podcast.body: In 2025, Andy Summers, along with Stuart Copeland, sued Sting for arranger's fees they believe are owed for "Every Breath You Take," arguing that his guitar arpeggio and "smoldering riff" were vital to the song's distinctive sound and enduring popularity. "Stings to police bandmates, guitarist Andy Summers and drummer Stuart Copeland have sued Sting for what they say they are owed for a ranger's fees on every breath you take."

podcast.title: Collaborations with Sting (1980s-1990s)
podcast.body: Andy Summers' "hypnotic guitar riffs" contributed to The Police's groove-oriented sound. Sting played guitar on several of Summers' solo projects in the late 1980s, and Summers returned the favor by playing bass and singing on a few of Sting's projects in the 1990s. "Sting actually played guitar on several Sting solo songs in the late 80s and Sting returned the favor by playing bass and singing on a few summers projects in the 90s."

podcast.title: Condition for Joining The Police
podcast.body: Summers agreed to join The Police on the condition that he would be the sole guitarist, which led to the firing of Henry Padovani. "When they asked him to join the police, he agreed on the condition that he would be the only guitarist."

podcast.title: Contribution to "Every Breath You Take"
podcast.body: Andy Summers was responsible for the famous "smoldering riff" and guitar arpeggio in "Every Breath You Take," elements that are considered arguably as important to the song's endurance as Sting's melody. "The guitar arpeggio, that famous smoldering riff which Andy Summers came up with himself and the cracking snare drum rhythm that Stuart Copeland devised."

podcast.title: Extensive Pre-Police Career
podcast.body: Prior to joining The Police, Andy Summers had an extensive career playing in bands since the mid-1960s, working as a studio musician, and backing other artists on tour, including a stint with The Animals in 1968. "He had been playing in band since the mid-1960s. He was also a studio guy and a guitarist who backed up other artists with their touring bands. That included a stint in the animals back in 1968."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Late Bloomers

podcast.title: Journeyman Guitarist
podcast.body: Andy Summers was described as a "journeyman guitarist with more experience than either" Sting or Stuart Copeland, possessing a "very accomplished resume" from playing with numerous bands in the 60s and early 70s. "But, while they were in the short-lived Strontym90, Sting and Stuart met and played with a journeyman guitarist with more experience than either of them, and a very accomplished resume."

podcast.title: Older Than Punk Contemporaries
podcast.body: At 36, when The Police broke through, Andy Summers was significantly older (10 to 15 years) than most of the band's punk and new wave contemporaries, a fact that was little noticed or cared about at the time. "At 36, he was far older than the police's punk and new wave contemporaries, 10 or 15 years older."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prior Performance Seen by Sting
podcast.body: Sting, as a teenager in Newcastle, had previously seen Andy Summers perform with Zoot Money's Psychedelic Band, a fact he only realized after meeting Summers later. "Sting even realized after meeting Summers that as a teenager in Newcastle, he'd seen Andy perform with Zoot Money's Psychedelic Band."

xref.title: Older Than Contemporaries
xref.body: The members of The Police were notably older than most of their post-punk and new wave peers when their debut album *Outlandos d'Amour* was released in 1978. Andy Summers, the guitarist, was 36, making him 10 to 15 years older than many contemporary artists, though few realized or cared. "But their members were actually a little older than their contemporaries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Late Bloomers

xref.title: Unique Guitar Playing Style
xref.body: Ian, the band's guitarist, developed a unique, self-taught playing style that combines rhythm and lead parts due to being the sole guitarist. He achieves this by playing in drop D tuning, which allows him to play bar chords with one finger while doing leads with the others, describing it as "almost like piano playing." He was influenced by clean players like Andy Summers and Mark Knopfler, as well as Tom Morello and Kim Thayil, and consciously avoided traditional playing. His style is considered "the most unique in the world." "I ended up trying to do both when I became the sole guitar player in this band. And by doing that, I found like dropping to D, I could play, I could play bar chords with one finger and then do a bunch of leads with the other."
